content: Postnatal depression is a clinical condition that significantly impacts many women and can also affect the development of their infants. Currently, there is limited evidence supporting safe and effective treatment or prevention strategies for this condition that are suitable for both mothers and their infants. Certain nutritional deficiencies in the diets of pregnant or postpartum women may contribute to the development of postnatal depression. Addressing these deficiencies through dietary supplementation could potentially prevent postnatal depression in some women. Examples of dietary supplements that have been proposed for this purpose include omega-3 fatty acids, iron, folate, S-adenosyl-L-methionine, cobalamin (vitamin B12), pyridoxine (vitamin B6), riboflavin (vitamin B2), vitamin D, and calcium. The objective of this review was to evaluate the potential benefits of dietary supplements in preventing postnatal depression, whether administered during pregnancy, after childbirth, or both. To achieve this, a search was conducted in the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register up to April 30, 2013. The review included randomized controlled trials involving women who were either pregnant or had given birth within the previous six weeks. These women were not experiencing depression or taking antidepressants at the start of the trials. The interventions studied included dietary supplements, either alone or in combination with other treatments, compared to placebo, standard clinical care, or other preventive measures. Two randomized controlled trials were included in the review. In the first trial, 100 microgram (µg) selenium yeast tablets were compared to placebo. The supplementation began in the first trimester and continued until delivery. A total of 179 women were randomized, but outcome data were only available for 85 participants. In the selenium group, 61 women completed the trial, with 44 completing the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS). In the placebo group, 64 women completed the trial, with 41 completing the EPDS. The study found that selenium supplementation had an effect on EPDS scores, but the results did not reach statistical significance (P = 0.07). The mean difference in EPDS scores was -1.90 (95% confidence interval [CI] -3.92 to 0.12) within eight weeks postpartum. However, the study was at high risk of attrition bias due to a significant number of participants withdrawing or not completing the EPDS. Additionally, the study did not report on any secondary outcomes. The second trial investigated the effects of docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) and eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) compared to placebo. This trial included 126 women at risk of postpartum depression, who were randomized into three groups: 42 received EPA, 42 received DHA, and 42 received placebo. Women with major depressive disorder, bipolar disorder, current substance abuse or dependence, suicidal ideation, or schizophrenia were excluded. Supplements or placebo were administered from 12 to 20 weeks of gestation until six to eight weeks postpartum. The primary outcome was the Beck Depression Inventory (BDI) score at six to eight weeks postpartum. No significant benefit was observed for EPA-rich fish oil (mean difference [MD] 0.70, 95% CI -1.78 to 3.18) or DHA-rich fish oil (MD 0.90, 95% CI -1.33 to 3.13) in preventing postpartum depression. Additionally, no significant difference was found when comparing EPA to DHA (MD -0.20, 95% CI -2.61 to 2.21). Secondary outcomes, including the presence of major depressive disorder, initiation of antidepressant use, maternal blood loss during delivery, and neonatal intensive care unit admissions, also showed no significant differences. In conclusion, the evidence is insufficient to support the use of selenium, DHA, or EPA for the prevention of postnatal depression. Furthermore, there is currently no evidence to recommend any other dietary supplement for this purpose.
